newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian call ends down, gilts rise in brisk trade.
newsitem.headline: Indian call ends down, gilts rise in brisk trade.

text.p: Indian call money ended Monday at 4.5 percent, down from opening quotes of 5.25-5.75 percent, on good liquidity, dealers said.
Call opened higher but eased as supply of funds was good and there was resistance from borrowers, they said.

"Liquidity with the banking system is good," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "Banks are flush with funds as credit offtake by commercial borrowers is poor. Central bank dollar purchases have also injected rupees into the system."
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has been buying dollars for nearly one year in an attempt to stem the rupee's rise against the U.S. currency, dealers said.
Strong dollar inflows and poor demand for the greenback have kept the rupee buoyant and threatened to affect Indian exports.
Dealers said prices of government securities ended up in brisk trade as low call money rates fuelled demand.

"Prices rose quite sharply...around 20-30 paise," said a dealer. "But later in the afternoon they came down slightly as there were fewer buyers at higher levels. There was probably some profit-taking at higher levels."
The 12.59 percent 2004 stock traded on Monday at 101.41 rupees against its last traded 101 the 12.14 percent 2000 at 101.66 against 101.30 dealers, said.
The 13.05 percent 2007 rose to 103 rupees from 102.20.
Treasury bill maturing on April 24 1998 traded at a yield of 8.85 percent, against its last traded 8.9 percent, dealers said.
